text: The LORD showed me this: two baskets of figs set out before the temple of the LORD. This was after Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had carried away from Jerusalem Jeconiah son of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, together with the officials of Judah, the craftsmen and the metalworkers, and had brought them to Babylon.
One basket held very good figs, like those that ripen first; the other held very bad figs, so bad they could not be eaten.
The LORD said to me, "What do you see, Jeremiah?" I answered, "Figs. The good ones are very good, and the bad ones are so bad they cannot be eaten."
Then the word of the LORD came to me:
This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Like these good figs, so I will look with favor on the exiles of Judah, whom I sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.

versions.text: This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: Like these good figs, so I will regard with favor the exiles of Judah whom I sent away from this place to the land of the Chaldeans.
versions.explanation: "Regard with favor the exiles" separates verb and object awkwardly for oral reading; "look with favor on" flows better. A comma before the relative clause also aids the reader's phrasing, since the clause is descriptive rather than restrictive.

text: I will keep my eyes on them for their good, and I will bring them back to this land. I will build them up and not tear them down; I will plant them and not uproot them.
I will give them a heart to know me, that I am the LORD. They will be my people, and I will be their God, for they will return to me with all their heart.

But like the bad figs, so bad they cannot be eaten—this is what the LORD says—so will I deal with Zedekiah king of Judah, his officials, and the remnant of Jerusalem, both those left in this land and those living in the land of Egypt.
I will make them a horror, a thing of evil, to all the kingdoms of the earth—a disgrace and a byword, an object of ridicule and cursing, in every place where I drive them.

versions.text: I will make them a horror and a disaster to all the kingdoms of the earth, a disgrace and a byword, an object of ridicule and cursing, in every place where I drive them.
versions.explanation: "A disaster" suggests the people suffer a calamity, whereas לְרָעָה here describes how the nations will view them (an evil, offensive thing). The dash also breaks the long list into two breath units for oral reading.

text: I will send the sword, famine, and plague against them until they are destroyed from the land I gave to them and to their ancestors.

versions.text: I will send the sword, famine, and plague against them until they are wiped from the land I gave to them and to their fathers.
versions.explanation: תֻּמָּם conveys being consumed or destroyed; "wiped from" is incomplete English (usually "wiped off" or "wiped out"). "Ancestors" renders אֲבוֹתֵיהֶם inclusively and reads naturally aloud.
